previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of chronic pancreatitis, vasculitis, and POTS was admitted for recurrent abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting consistent with a flare of her chronic pancreatitis. She initially presented with right upper quadrant pain that progressed to epigastric pain, associated with bilious emesis and an episode of blood-tinged vomitus. She was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, IV Dilaudid for pain, and Zofran for nausea. Her lipase was only mildly elevated, but clinical presentation supported a pancreatic flare. She gradually improved, tolerated advancement to a regular diet, and successfully transitioned to oral pain and nausea medications. Methotrexate was administered during admission. She was discharged home in stable condition with controlled pain, tolerating oral intake, and instructions to continue her medications, including pancreatic enzyme supplements and new stool softeners to prevent opioid-induced constipation.

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is a ___ year old woman with PMHx chronic 
pancreatitis/vasculitis who presented with abdominal pain, 
nausea, and 1 episode hematemesis.
  
#. Abdominal pain: The patient's abdominal pain was consistent 
with typical flare of pancreatitis/vasculitis. Pt is being 
managed by her PCP and GI - considering increasing methotrexate 
dose and prednisone to control flares. The patient was kept NPO 
for several days, and diet was advanced slowly. Pain was 
controlled with IV Dilaudid until she was able to tolerate PO 
meds, then switched to PO Dilaudid. She was kept on IVF ___ 
NS) while NPO. When patient was able to tolerate sips and oral 
meds for a full day, she was monitored on clears for a full day. 
She was discharged after tolerating several meals of full 
liquids. She was instructed to continue full liquids for another 
day, then keep a bland diet for the next 2 weeks. 
   
#. Hematemesis: The patient had hematemesis, most likely ___ 
___ tear, as the pt had episode of hematemesis after several 
minutes of vomiting and also has a h/o ___ tears in 
the past. The patient had several more episodes of hematemesis 
during the first few days of her hospitalization. HCT was 
monitored closely and remained relatively stable, and the 
patient was asymptomatic. She patient did not require 
transfusion during the hospitalization. She was kept on IV PPI. 
Hematemesis resolved several days prior to discharge. 
   
#. Hypotension: The patient has low BP at baseline (SBP 
___. She had a drop in BP to ___ after a dose of 
Betaxolol. She was given IV boluses and responded appropriately. 
BP on discharge was back to baseline. 
   
#. Constipation: The patient came in with constipation, related 
to combination of low PO intake and administration of opiates. 
Pt was given Bisacodyl PR and had several BM during the 
hospitalization. 
   
#. Sjogren's: The patient was continued on her home medications 
when she was able to tolerated PO meds.
   
#. POTS: The patient was continued on her home medications: 
betaxolol, fludrocortisone, and midodrine. Betaxolol was held 
after episode of hypotension to ___. BP was back to baseline 
on discharge. 
   
#. Anxiety: The patient was continued on her home medications 
amitriptyline and escitalopram.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital with abdominal pain, nausea, 
and vomiting. You also had several episodes where you vomited 
blood, which is thought to be secondary to ___ tears 
in your esophagus from frequent vomiting. Your hematocrit stayed 
stable, and you did not require a blood transfusion. You were 
given intravenous fluids, Zofran and Ativan to control the 
nausea, and Dilaudid for pain control. Your nausea has resolved, 
and you are currently tolerating an oral diet.
   
You had several episodes of hypotension, thought to be secondary 
to the Betaxolol. Your blood pressure improved with more 
intravenous fluids. 
   
No changes were made to your medications.
   
If you experience worsening abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, 
especially vomiting blood, shortness of breath, chest pain, 
lightheadedness, or any other concerning symptoms, please call 
your primary care doctor or return to the emergency department.
